newsitem.title: CHINA: China army in drive for better logistics.
newsitem.headline: China army in drive for better logistics.

text.p: China's People's Liberation Army (PLA) will target elite units in a drive to improve logistics equipment and facilities in the nation's rapidly modernising armed forces, the China Daily said on Friday.

Since 1991, the PLA had developed more than 400 types of logistics equipment in areas such as communications, fuel supply, transportation and surgical treatment, it quoted Wang Xiangwen of the Science, Technology and Equipment Division of the PLA's General Logistics Department as saying.
"China... is ready to use them in equipping crack troops," the newspaper said.
It was important to improve the efficiency and capability of logistics equipment because of the large amount of supplies needed to fight modern wars, it quote Wang as saying.
"The development of logistics equipment should go side by side with the development of weapons," he said.
Among the new equipment was the S100 field hospital, which boasted surgical and X-ray equipment, satellite communications and computer facilities, he said.
The PLA had also developed a method of providing seaborne supplies to military vessels on heavy seas, he said but gave no further details.
China is eager to expand the range of its navy, which has in the past been limited to little more than a coastal defence role.
The PLA would strengthen cooperation and exchange with foreign counterparts in order to learn foreign technology and to speed the modernisation drive, Wang he said.
Foreign experts would be invited to lecture and train Chinese technicians at an international exhibition on military logistics equipment and technology in Beijing in May next year, he said.

Shocked by the display of high-technology warfare put on by Western powers during the 1991 Gulf War, China has been trying to modernise its backward armed forces, much of which still depend on obsolete equipment of Soviet design.
State media reported this week the PLA would gradually adopt a new generation of light armaments already carried by its crack Hong Kong garrison.

Made domestically with advanced materials and manufacturing techniques, these small-bore automatic rifles and machine guns were smaller, lighter, more powerful and have a longer range than comparable foreign weapons, newspapers said.

China has said it plans to trim its three-million-strong force by 500,000 troops and boost its defence budget by 14.7 percent to $9.7 billion in 1997. Analysts say the official budget accounts for only a fraction of actual defence spending.
